Acronyms 206

3DES
Triple Data Encryption Standard. DES applied three times; legacy and slow, replaced by AES.
802.1X
IEEE 802.1X. Port-based network access control: a device must authenticate before the switch port or Wi-Fi passes traffic.
AAA
Authentication, authorization, and accounting. Prove who you are, decide what you may do, record what you did.
ABAC
Attribute-based access control. Access decisions based on attributes of the user, resource, and context, such as time and location.
ACL
Access control list. An ordered list of permit and deny rules on a router, firewall, or file system.
AES
Advanced Encryption Standard. The standard symmetric cipher, with 128, 192, or 256-bit keys.
AES-128
AES with a 128-bit key. The standard-strength AES, secure and fast.
AES-256
AES with a 256-bit key. The high-strength AES used for data at rest and sensitive sessions.
AES-CCMP
AES in CCMP mode. The AES-based encryption WPA2 uses for Wi-Fi.
AH
Authentication Header. The IPsec protocol that provides integrity and authentication without encryption.
ALE
Annualized loss expectancy. The expected yearly cost of a risk: SLE times ARO.
AP
Access point. The radio that bridges Wi-Fi clients onto the wired network.
API
Application programming interface. The defined way one program talks to another, such as the web endpoints a cloud service exposes.
APT
Advanced persistent threat. A well-funded, skilled, patient attacker, usually a nation-state, that stays hidden for a long time.
ARO
Annualized rate of occurrence. How many times per year an incident is expected to happen.
ARP
Address Resolution Protocol. Finds the MAC address that goes with a known IPv4 address on the local segment.
ASLR
Address space layout randomization. Randomizes where programs load in memory so exploits cannot predict addresses.
AUP
Acceptable use policy. The rules for how staff may use company systems and data.
AV
Asset value. What an asset is worth, the first number in quantitative risk analysis (SLE = AV x EF). Also: Antivirus. Software that detects, quarantines, and removes malware using signatures, heuristics, and behavior.
BEC
Business email compromise. Fraud by email impersonating an executive or vendor to redirect payments.
BIA
Business impact analysis. Identifies critical functions and what an outage of each would cost, setting RTO and RPO.
BPA
Business partnership agreement. How partners share responsibilities, profits, and liabilities.
BYOD
Bring your own device. Staff use personal phones and laptops for work.
CA
Certificate authority. The trusted entity that signs certificates.
CEO
Chief executive officer. The top executive; the person impersonated in whaling and business email compromise.
CFO
Chief financial officer. The executive in charge of money; a common target and impersonation in payment fraud.
CI
Continuous integration. Every code change is automatically built and tested when it is committed.
CIA
Confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The three goals of security: keep data secret, keep it correct, keep it reachable.
CIS
Center for Internet Security. The organization that publishes hardening benchmarks and the CIS Controls.
COPE
Corporate-owned, personally enabled. The company buys the device and lets staff use it personally.
CPU
Central processing unit. The processor that executes instructions.
CRL
Certificate revocation list. A signed list of revoked certificate serial numbers published by a CA.
CSR
Certificate signing request. The file containing a public key and identity that you send to a CA to get a certificate.
CSRF
Cross-site request forgery. Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request the user did not intend.
CVE
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. The public identifier for a known vulnerability, such as CVE-2024-12345.
CVSS
Common Vulnerability Scoring System. A 0 to 10 severity score for a vulnerability.
CYOD
Choose your own device. Staff pick from a list of approved devices the company then owns and manages.
DAC
Discretionary access control. The owner of a resource decides who may access it.
DBA
Database administrator. The person who runs the database servers.
DDoS
Distributed denial of service. Many sources, usually a botnet, flood a target at once.
DER
Distinguished Encoding Rules. The binary format for certificates and keys.
DES
Data Encryption Standard. The 1970s 56-bit block cipher; broken by brute force, do not use.
DHCP
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. Hands out IP addresses, masks, gateways, and DNS servers automatically (UDP 67 and 68).
DKIM
DomainKeys Identified Mail. Outgoing mail is digitally signed; the public key is published in DNS.
DLP
Data loss prevention. Tools that detect and block sensitive data leaving by email, web, USB, or cloud.
DMARC
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance. A DNS policy telling receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF or DKIM, and where to send reports.
DMZ
Demilitarized zone. A screened subnet between the internet and the internal network for public-facing servers.
DNS
Domain Name System. Translates names such as www.example.com into IP addresses (UDP 53, TCP 53 for zone transfers).
DNSSEC
DNS Security Extensions. Digital signatures on DNS records so a resolver can tell an answer was not forged.
DoH
DNS over HTTPS. DNS queries carried inside HTTPS on TCP 443 so they cannot be read or altered in transit.
DoS
Denial of service. One source floods or crashes a target so it cannot serve users.
DoT
DNS over TLS. DNS queries encrypted with TLS on TCP 853.
DSA
Digital Signature Algorithm. A government-standard signature algorithm; used less than RSA and ECDSA today.
EAP
Extensible Authentication Protocol. The framework that carries authentication methods inside 802.1X.
EAP-FAST
EAP Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling. Cisco's tunneled EAP method using a protected access credential instead of a certificate.
EAP-TLS
EAP with Transport Layer Security. Certificate-based authentication on both sides; the strongest Wi-Fi and wired 802.1X method.
EAP-TTLS
EAP with Tunneled TLS. A server certificate builds a TLS tunnel, then the client authenticates inside it with a password or other method.
ECC
Elliptic curve cryptography. Public-key cryptography that gives RSA-level strength with much shorter keys, ideal for phones and IoT.
ECDHE
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. Key exchange with a fresh elliptic curve key per session, giving forward secrecy.
ECDSA
Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. Digital signatures using elliptic curve keys.
EDR
Endpoint detection and response. Endpoint agents that record activity, detect attacks, and let responders isolate and clean the machine.
EF
Exposure factor. The fraction of an asset's value lost in one incident.
ESP
Encapsulating Security Payload. The IPsec protocol that encrypts and authenticates the payload.
FIDO2
Fast Identity Online 2. Passwordless or second-factor authentication with a hardware security key or device biometrics.
FIM
File integrity monitoring. Alerts when critical files or configurations change.
FTP
File Transfer Protocol. Plaintext file transfer on TCP 21 (control) and 20 (data); replace with SFTP or FTPS.
FTPS
FTP Secure. FTP wrapped in TLS, ports 990 and 989 (implicit) or 21 with an upgrade (explicit).
GB
Gigabyte. About a billion bytes; the unit for RAM, storage, and data caps.
GCMP
Galois/Counter Mode Protocol. The stronger AES encryption mode used by WPA3.
GPS
Global Positioning System. Satellite positioning, also used as a stratum 0 time reference.
HMAC
Hash-based message authentication code. A keyed hash that proves a message came from someone with the key and was not altered.
HR
Human resources. The department that hires and separates staff; its system should drive account provisioning and removal.
HSM
Hardware security module. A tamper-resistant appliance or card that generates, stores, and uses cryptographic keys.
HTTP
Hypertext Transfer Protocol. Web traffic in the clear on TCP 80.
HTTPS
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. HTTP inside TLS on TCP 443.
IaaS
Infrastructure as a service. The provider supplies virtual machines, storage, and networks; you manage the operating system and up.
IaC
Infrastructure as code. Defining networks and servers in files that tools build automatically and repeatably.
ICS
Industrial control system. The general term for computers that run physical processes; SCADA is one kind.
ID
Identifier or identification. A name or number that uniquely labels a user, device, session, or record.
IDS
Intrusion detection system. Watches a copy of the traffic and alerts on attacks; cannot block them.
IKE
Internet Key Exchange. Negotiates the keys and security associations for IPsec; UDP 500, and 4500 through NAT.
IMAP
Internet Message Access Protocol. Reads mail that stays on the server, synced across devices; TCP 143, secure 993.
IMAPS
IMAP Secure. IMAP over TLS on TCP 993.
iOS
iPhone operating system. Apple's mobile operating system for iPhone.
IoT
Internet of Things. Networked devices such as cameras, sensors, thermostats, and smart TVs.
IP
Internet Protocol. The Layer 3 protocol that addresses and routes packets between networks.
IPS
Intrusion prevention system. Sits inline and blocks attacks as they pass.
IPsec
Internet Protocol Security. The suite that encrypts and authenticates IP packets for VPNs.
ISAC
Information sharing and analysis center. An industry group where members share threat intelligence.
IT
Information technology. Computers, networks, and the people who run them.
KMS
Key management service. A managed, usually cloud-hosted, service that creates, stores, rotates, and controls access to encryption keys.
LACP
Link Aggregation Control Protocol. Negotiates bundling several physical links into one logical link (802.1AX, formerly 802.3ad).
LAN
Local area network. One site's network: a building, floor, or campus that one organization owns and runs.
LDAP
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Queries a directory such as Active Directory for users and groups; TCP 389, secure 636.
LDAPS
LDAP Secure. LDAP over TLS on TCP 636.
LTE
Long-Term Evolution. 4G cellular data; the workhorse mobile broadband standard.
MAC
Media access control (address). The 48-bit Layer 2 hardware address of a network interface, which a switch uses to forward frames. Also: Mandatory access control. The access control model where the system assigns classification labels that users cannot change.
MD5
Message Digest 5. A 128-bit hash that is broken: collisions can be manufactured; recognize, never recommend.
MDM
Mobile device management. Software that enrolls phones and tablets and enforces policy: passcodes, encryption, apps, remote wipe.
MFA
Multi-factor authentication. Two or more different kinds of proof: something you know, have, are, or where you are.
MIME
Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions. The standard that lets email carry attachments and non-text content.
MOA
Memorandum of agreement. A more formal, sometimes binding, statement of what parties agree to do.
MOU
Memorandum of understanding. A non-binding statement of intent and roles between parties.
MPLS
Multiprotocol Label Switching. A provider WAN that forwards by short labels instead of IP lookups, with traffic engineering and QoS.
ms
Millisecond. One thousandth of a second; latency and response times.
MSA
Master service agreement. The umbrella contract covering a whole vendor relationship; individual jobs hang off it.
MTBF
Mean time between failures. The average running time before a component fails; a reliability measure.
MTTR
Mean time to repair. The average time to fix a failure and restore service.
NAC
Network access control. Checks a device's identity and health before letting it onto the network.
NAT-T
NAT traversal. Wraps IPsec in UDP 4500 so it can pass through address translation.
NDA
Non-disclosure agreement. A contract that keeps shared information confidential.
NGFW
Next-generation firewall. A firewall that identifies applications and users, and includes intrusion prevention.
NTP
Network Time Protocol. Synchronizes clocks across the network (UDP 123); wrong time breaks Kerberos, certificates, and logs.
NTS
Network Time Security. Authentication and integrity for NTP so time cannot be spoofed.
OAuth
Open Authorization. Lets a user grant an application limited access to their account on another service without sharing the password.
OCSP
Online Certificate Status Protocol. A real-time query to the CA asking whether one certificate is revoked.
OS
Operating system. The software that manages hardware and runs applications: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android.
OSINT
Open-source intelligence. Information gathered from public sources: websites, social media, records, DNS.
P7B
PKCS #7 bundle. A file holding a certificate chain with no private key.
PBKDF2
Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2. Stretches a password with many hash rounds so guessing is slow.
PEAP
Protected EAP. A server certificate creates a TLS tunnel and the user's password is checked inside it.
PEM
Privacy Enhanced Mail (format). The Base64 text format for certificates and keys, with BEGIN and END lines.
PFX
Personal Information Exchange. A password-protected bundle holding a certificate and its private key (also .p12).
PIN
Personal identification number. A short numeric secret, a something-you-know factor.
PKI
Public key infrastructure. The system of certificate authorities, certificates, and revocation that makes public keys trustworthy.
POP3
Post Office Protocol version 3. Downloads mail to one device and usually deletes it from the server; TCP 110, secure 995.
POP3S
POP3 Secure. POP3 over TLS on TCP 995.
PSK
Pre-shared key. One shared passphrase for everyone on a Wi-Fi network (Personal mode).
RA
Registration authority. The part of a PKI that verifies identities before the CA signs.
RADIUS
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. The AAA server behind Wi-Fi Enterprise, VPNs, and 802.1X; UDP 1812 and 1813.
RAID
Redundant array of independent disks. Combining disks for speed, capacity, or fault tolerance: 0 stripe, 1 mirror, 5 stripe with parity, 6 double parity, 10 mirrored stripes.
RAM
Random-access memory. The working memory that holds running programs and data; lost at power off.
RAT
Remote access trojan. Malware that opens a back door so an attacker can control the machine.
RBAC
Role-based access control. Permissions are assigned to roles, and users get roles.
RC4
Rivest Cipher 4. A fast stream cipher used in WEP and old TLS; broken and deprecated.
RDP
Remote Desktop Protocol. Microsoft's remote graphical desktop on TCP 3389.
RFID
Radio-frequency identification. Tags read by radio for badges, inventory, and asset tracking.
RPO
Recovery point objective. The maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.
RSA
Rivest, Shamir, Adleman. The classic public-key algorithm for encryption and digital signatures.
RTO
Recovery time objective. The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after failure.
RTOS
Real-time operating system. An operating system that guarantees responses within strict time limits, used in embedded and control devices.
RTP
Real-time Transport Protocol. Carries the actual voice and video packets of a call, over UDP.
SaaS
Software as a service. Complete applications delivered over the web, such as email and office suites.
SAE
Simultaneous authentication of equals. The WPA3 Personal handshake that resists offline password guessing.
SAML
Security Assertion Markup Language. An XML standard for passing authentication between an identity provider and a web application (enterprise SSO).
SAN
Subject alternative name. The certificate field listing every hostname the certificate is valid for.
SASE
Secure access service edge. SD-WAN networking plus cloud-delivered security (firewall, web gateway, ZTNA, CASB) as one service.
SCADA
Supervisory control and data acquisition. Systems that monitor and control industrial processes such as power, water, and manufacturing.
SCAP
Security Content Automation Protocol. Standard formats that let tools check systems against security benchmarks automatically.
SD-WAN
Software-defined wide area network. Steers traffic across several cheap links (broadband, LTE, MPLS) by policy from a central controller.
SDLC
Software development life cycle. The phases of building software: plan, design, code, test, deploy, maintain.
SDN
Software-defined networking. Separates the control plane (decisions) from the data plane (forwarding) and centralizes control.
SFTP
SSH File Transfer Protocol. File transfer inside an SSH session, TCP 22.
SHA
Secure Hash Algorithm. The family of hash functions: SHA-1 (deprecated), SHA-2 (SHA-256, the standard), SHA-3.
SHA-1
Secure Hash Algorithm 1. A 160-bit hash, deprecated because collisions have been found.
SHA-2
Secure Hash Algorithm 2. The current hash family, including SHA-256 and SHA-512.
SHA-256
Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit. The standard hash today: a 256-bit fingerprint of any input.
SHA-3
Secure Hash Algorithm 3. A newer hash standard with a different internal design from SHA-2.
SIEM
Security information and event management. Collects logs from everything, correlates them, and raises alerts.
SIP
Session Initiation Protocol. Sets up and tears down voice and video calls; port 5060, or 5061 with TLS.
SLA
Service level agreement. The contract stating measurable service commitments, such as 99.9% uptime.
SLE
Single loss expectancy. The cost of one occurrence of a risk: asset value times exposure factor.
SMB
Server Message Block. Windows file and printer sharing on TCP 445.
SMS
Short Message Service. Text messages; used for one-time codes and also a phishing channel (smishing).
SMTP
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Sends email between servers on TCP 25; clients submit on 587 with TLS.
SMTPS
SMTP Secure. SMTP with TLS, port 465 (implicit) or 587 with STARTTLS.
SNMP
Simple Network Management Protocol. Polls and receives alerts from network devices (UDP 161 polls, 162 traps).
SOW
Statement of work. Defines one specific piece of work: deliverables, timeline, and price.
SPF
Sender Policy Framework. A DNS TXT record listing which servers may send mail for a domain.
SQL
Structured Query Language. The language used to query databases; also the name of the servers on TCP 1433 (Microsoft) and 3306 (MySQL).
SRTP
Secure Real-time Transport Protocol. Encrypted RTP for voice and video.
SSH
Secure Shell. Encrypted remote command-line access and file transfer on TCP 22; replaces Telnet and FTP.
SSID
Service set identifier. The Wi-Fi network name that access points broadcast and clients join.
SSL
Secure Sockets Layer. The predecessor of TLS; every version is deprecated.
SSO
Single sign-on. Log in once and reach many systems without signing in again.
SSRF
Server-side request forgery. Makes the web server itself fetch a URL the attacker supplies, often reaching internal systems.
SY0-701
CompTIA Security+ exam SY0-701. The current version of the Security+ certification exam.
TACACS+
Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus. Cisco's AAA protocol for device administration on TCP 49; encrypts the whole payload and separates authentication from authorization.
TCP
Transmission Control Protocol. Reliable, ordered, connection-based transport: three-way handshake, acknowledgments, retransmission.
TFTP
Trivial File Transfer Protocol. Bare-bones UDP 69 file transfer with no login, used for firmware and config files.
TKIP
Temporal Key Integrity Protocol. WPA's per-packet keying scheme; deprecated.
TLS
Transport Layer Security. The encryption layer under HTTPS and most secure protocols; use 1.2 or 1.3.
TOC
Time of check. The moment a program verifies a condition; in a race condition, before it acts on it.
TOU
Time of use. The moment a program acts on a condition it checked earlier.
TPM
Trusted Platform Module. A security chip on the motherboard that stores keys and measurements; required for BitLocker and Windows 11.
TV
Television. A display or broadcast receiver; smart TVs are IoT devices.
UBA
User behavior analytics. Baselines what each user normally does and flags deviations.
UEFI
Unified Extensible Firmware Interface. Modern firmware that replaces BIOS: GPT disks, Secure Boot, mouse-driven setup.
UPS
Uninterruptible power supply. A battery unit that keeps equipment running through a power cut and conditions the power.
URL
Uniform resource locator. A web address such as https://www.example.com/page.
USB
Universal Serial Bus. The standard port for peripherals, storage, and charging.
UTM
Unified threat management. One appliance bundling firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, content filtering, and VPN.
VLAN
Virtual local area network. A logical LAN on a switch: ports in different VLANs are separate broadcast domains.
VM
Virtual machine. A complete computer running as software on a hypervisor.
VPN
Virtual private network. An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network such as the internet.
WAF
Web application firewall. A firewall that understands HTTP and blocks attacks on web applications such as SQL injection and XSS.
WAN
Wide area network. Connects LANs across cities or countries, usually over links leased from a provider.
WEP
Wired Equivalent Privacy. The original Wi-Fi encryption, broken in minutes; never use it.
Wi-Fi
Wireless fidelity. The trade name for IEEE 802.11 wireless networking.
WO
Work order. A short authorization for one specific job.
WPA
Wi-Fi Protected Access. The interim fix for WEP that used TKIP; deprecated.
WPA2
Wi-Fi Protected Access 2. Wi-Fi security using AES with CCMP; still common and acceptable.
WPA3
Wi-Fi Protected Access 3. The current Wi-Fi security standard: SAE in Personal mode, stronger encryption, protected management frames.
XDR
Extended detection and response. EDR extended across endpoints, network, cloud, and email into one correlated view.
XML
Extensible Markup Language. A text format for structured data, used by SAML, SOAP, and many configuration files.
XSS
Cross-site scripting. An attacker's script runs in other users' browsers because a site echoes untrusted input.

22%

Cryptography 25

Symmetric
One shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, bulk data. AES (128, 192, 256-bit), 3DES (legacy), ChaCha20, Blowfish
Asymmetric
Public key encrypts or verifies, private key decrypts or signs. Slow, used for key exchange and signatures. RSA, ECC (smaller keys, same strength), DSA, ECDSA
Key exchange
Diffie-Hellman and ECDHE agree on a shared key over an open channel. Ephemeral keys give perfect forward secrecy
Hashing
One-way fixed-length fingerprint: MD5 128-bit (broken), SHA-1 160-bit (deprecated), SHA-256, SHA-3. HMAC adds a key for authenticity
Salting
Random data added to a password before hashing so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables fail
Key stretching
Make hashing slow on purpose: PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2
Digital signature
Hash the message, encrypt the hash with the private key. Proves integrity, authenticity, and non-repudiation
Key length
Longer is stronger; AES-256 over AES-128, RSA 2048 minimum, ECC 256 is comparable to RSA 3072
Blockchain
Open public ledger: chained hashed blocks, tamper-evident, distributed
Transport encryption
TLS 1.2 and 1.3 for web and mail, IPsec for VPNs, SSH for shells. Deprecated: SSL, TLS 1.0 and 1.1
Full-disk
The whole drive; protects a lost laptop
Partition or volume
One partition or logical volume
File
Individual files
Database
The whole database
Record
Individual fields or rows, such as card numbers
Certificate authority (CA)
Issues and signs certificates; the root of trust
Registration authority
Verifies identity before the CA issues
CSR
Certificate signing request: the public key plus identity sent to the CA
CRL
Certificate revocation list, downloaded periodically; can be stale
OCSP
Real-time revocation check of one certificate; OCSP stapling has the server include a fresh response
Self-signed
Not signed by a trusted CA; browsers warn; internal use only
Third-party
Issued by a public CA; trusted by browsers
Wildcard
*.example.com covers every subdomain at one level
SAN
Subject alternative name: several names on one certificate
Formats
PEM (Base64 text, .crt .pem), DER (binary), PFX or P12 (with private key), P7B (chain, no private key)

Threat actors, vectors, and social engineering 19

Message-based
Email, SMS, instant messaging
Image-based and file-based
Malicious images, macros in documents, executables
Voice call
Vishing
Removable device
USB drops
Vulnerable software
Client-based (agent installed) versus agentless
Unsupported systems
End-of-life operating systems and applications
Unsecure networks
Open wireless, unmanaged wired ports, Bluetooth
Open service ports, default credentials
Exposed services, unchanged admin passwords
Supply chain
Managed service providers, vendors, suppliers
Phishing
Fraudulent email to steal credentials or deliver malware
Vishing, smishing
The same by voice call, by text message
Spear phishing, whaling
Targeted at a person; targeted at an executive
Business email compromise
Attacker uses or imitates a real business account to redirect payments
Pretexting
An invented story that justifies the request
Impersonation, brand impersonation
Pretending to be a person; pretending to be a company
Watering hole
Compromise a site the targets already visit
Typosquatting
Look-alike domain names catching mistyped URLs
Misinformation, disinformation
False content spread unknowingly; spread deliberately
Tailgating, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving
Following through a door; watching a screen; reading the trash

Vulnerabilities 11

Application
Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (time-of-check to time-of-use), malicious update
Operating system
Unpatched services, weak defaults
Web-based
SQL injection (' OR 1=1), cross-site scripting (script in a page other users load)
Hardware
Firmware flaws, end-of-life, legacy devices
Virtualization
VM escape (guest reaches the host), resource reuse (data left in reallocated memory or storage)
Cloud-specific
Misconfigured storage, shared-tenant risks, exposed APIs
Supply chain
Service provider, hardware provider, software provider
Cryptographic
Weak or deprecated algorithms, short keys, bad implementations
Misconfiguration
Open ports, default settings, excessive permissions
Mobile
Side loading (apps from outside the store), jailbreaking or rooting
Zero-day
Known to attackers before a patch exists

Attacks and indicators 8

Ransomware
Files encrypted, payment demanded
Trojan
Hidden inside a wanted program; remote access trojan gives control
Worm
Spreads by itself across the network
Virus
Attaches to files, needs a user action to spread
Spyware, keylogger
Watches activity; records keystrokes
Bloatware
Unwanted preinstalled software, expands attack surface
Logic bomb
Triggers on a date or event
Rootkit
Hides at kernel or firmware level; survives reboots, evades antivirus

Security architecture 12

Security zones
Trusted, untrusted, screened subnet (DMZ) for public-facing servers
Attack surface
Everything reachable; shrink it
Fail-open versus fail-closed
Fail-open keeps traffic flowing when the control fails (availability); fail-closed blocks (security)
Active versus passive
Inline (can block, can bottleneck) versus tap or monitor port (sees a copy, alerts only)
Jump server
Hardened host you go through to reach protected systems
Proxy server
Forward proxy for clients; reverse proxy in front of servers
IPS versus IDS
Inline and blocks versus out of band and alerts
Load balancer
Spreads traffic; active-active or active-passive
Sensors
Collect traffic or logs for monitoring
Port security
802.1X authentication on switch ports and Wi-Fi, using EAP (EAP-TLS with certificates is strongest; PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST)
Firewall types
WAF (Layer 7, protects web apps), UTM (all-in-one), NGFW (application-aware, user-aware), Layer 4 (ports) versus Layer 7 (content)
Secure communication
VPN and remote access; tunneling with TLS or IPsec; SD-WAN; SASE (network plus cloud security)

Data protection 9

Regulated
Law or regulation governs it: health, payment card, personal data
Trade secret, intellectual property
Formulas, source code, designs
Legal information, financial information
Contracts, litigation; ledgers, filings
Human-readable versus non-human-readable
Documents versus binaries and encrypted blobs
Public
Anyone may see it
Private, sensitive
Internal; harm if leaked
Confidential
Limited to those who need it
Restricted
Tightly controlled, often regulated
Critical
The organization cannot function without it

Resilience and recovery 12

Load balancing versus clustering
Spreads requests across servers; servers act as one system with failover
Hot site
Running mirror, minutes to switch, most expensive
Warm site
Equipment ready, data restored on failover, hours
Cold site
Space and power only, days
Geographic dispersion
Sites far enough apart that one disaster cannot hit both
Platform diversity, multi-cloud
Different vendors so one flaw or outage does not take everything
Continuity of operations
Keep the business running through the incident
Capacity planning
People, technology, infrastructure sized for growth and surge
Testing
Tabletop (talk through), failover (actually switch), simulation (drill), parallel processing (run both and compare)
Backups
Onsite and offsite, frequency, encryption, snapshots, replication, journaling (log every change), tested recovery
Full, incremental, differential
Everything; changes since the last backup of any kind (small, slow restore); changes since the last full (bigger, faster restore)
Power
UPS bridges to the generator; generator for long outages

Securing resources and monitoring 22

Identification
Vulnerability scans (credentialed sees more), application analysis static and dynamic, package monitoring, threat feeds (OSINT, proprietary, ISACs, dark web), penetration testing, responsible disclosure and bug bounty, system and process audits
Analysis
Confirm (false positive, false negative), prioritize with CVSS and CVE, classification, exposure factor, environmental variables, industry and organizational impact, risk tolerance
Response
Patch, cyber insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, documented exceptions and exemptions
Validation
Rescan, audit, verify
Reporting
Trends, open items, time to remediate
None
0.0
Low
0.1 to 3.9
Medium
4.0 to 6.9
High
7.0 to 8.9
Critical
9.0 to 10.0
Firewall rules, access lists, ports and protocols, screened subnets
Allow only what is needed between zones
IDS/IPS trends and signatures
Detect known patterns; tune for trends
Web filter
Agent-based or centralized proxy; URL scanning, content categorization, block rules, reputation
Operating system security
Group Policy on Windows, SELinux on Linux
Secure protocols
Pick the encrypted port and transport: SSH not Telnet, HTTPS not HTTP, SFTP not FTP, SNMPv3, LDAPS, DoH or DoT
DNS filtering
Block known-bad domains at resolution
Email security
SPF (allowed senders), DKIM (signed mail), DMARC (policy for failures), email gateway
File integrity monitoring
Alert when critical files change
DLP
Prevent sensitive data from leaving by email, USB, or upload
NAC
Check device health before granting network access
EDR and XDR
Endpoint detection and response; extended across network and cloud
User behavior analytics
Baseline each user, alert on deviation

Identity and access management 12

Provisioning and deprovisioning
Create access on hire, remove it on exit; the classic offboarding failure is a still-active account
Identity proofing
Verify a person is who they claim before issuing credentials
Federation
One organization trusts another's identities
SSO protocols
SAML (XML, enterprise web SSO), OAuth (authorization delegation), OpenID Connect (authentication on OAuth), LDAP (directory), Kerberos (tickets, Windows domains)
Attestation
Confirming that a device or account state is what it claims
Mandatory (MAC)
Labels and clearances set by the system; users cannot change them; military
Discretionary (DAC)
The owner decides who gets access; file permissions
Role-based (RBAC)
Permissions attach to roles, users to roles
Rule-based
Fixed rules such as firewall ACLs or time limits
Attribute-based (ABAC)
Decisions from attributes: department, location, device, time
Time-of-day restrictions
Access only during set hours
Least privilege
Only what the job needs

Incident response and forensics 7

Firewall logs
Allowed and blocked connections
Application logs
Errors, logins, transactions
Endpoint logs
Processes, files, EDR alerts
OS-specific logs
Windows Event logs, Linux syslog and auth logs
IPS/IDS logs
Matched signatures
Network logs, metadata
Flows, DNS, headers
Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards, packet captures
State, trends, and raw evidence

Governance, risk, and compliance 17

Asset value (AV)
What the asset is worth
Exposure factor (EF)
Fraction of value lost in one incident
Single loss expectancy
SLE = AV x EF
Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO)
How many times per year
Annualized loss expectancy
ALE = SLE x ARO
Qualitative versus quantitative
High/medium/low ratings versus dollars and probabilities
Assessment cadence
Ad hoc, recurring, one-time, continuous
Risk register
List of risks with key risk indicators, owners, and thresholds
Risk tolerance and appetite
How much variance is acceptable; appetite is expansionary, conservative, or neutral
Strategies
Transfer (insurance), accept (with exemption or exception), avoid (stop the activity), mitigate (add controls)
Business impact analysis
RTO (time to restore), RPO (data loss allowed), MTTR (mean repair time), MTBF (mean time between failures)
SLA
Measurable service levels and penalties
MOA, MOU
Agreement of intent; MOU less formal
MSA
Master agreement covering the relationship; work orders hang off it
WO / SOW
Work order or statement of work for one job
NDA
Confidentiality
BPA
Business partnership agreement: profits, responsibilities
